title: Theorem A
body_md:
Let $(R,\theta)$ satisfy the preceding assumptions.
Every automorphism of $E$, and every automorphism of $G$, has a
unique expression
\[
 \varphi=i_g\circ f_*,
 \qquad
 g\in G,\quad f\in\operatorname{Aut}(R,\theta).
\]
Every automorphism of $G_{\mathrm{sc}}=E_{\mathrm{sc}}$ is a
composition of a strictly inner automorphism, a diagonal
automorphism, and a ring automorphism induced by an element of
$\operatorname{Aut}(R,\theta)$.
Conversely, each such composition is an automorphism of the
corresponding group.
head: environment

title: Outline of the proof
body_md:
We separate normalization of a finite family of constant elements
from recovery of the arbitrary root parameters.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{1. Normalize the standard frame.}
For $\varphi\in\operatorname{Aut}E$, consider
\[
 \mathcal F(R)=(x_\lambda(1))_{\lambda\in\Phi_\rho},
\]
called the standard frame.
Normal structure allows reduction modulo $J$, and the field
automorphism theorem describes the residual action.
We lift and remove only its conjugating factor: the residual
coefficient automorphism already fixes the frame.
The resulting automorphism $\varphi_1$ therefore has standard
reductions on $\mathcal F(R)$.

On the $78$-dimensional Chevalley module $L_R$, one averaging over
a finite $2$-subgroup fixes the toral involutions and a chosen family
of Weyl elements simultaneously.
We then normalize the remaining Weyl elements and one complete
constant short-root matrix.
Weyl conjugation gives the other constant short-root elements, and
short--short commutators determine the constant long-root elements
from their squares.
The accumulated change of basis
$C_0\in\operatorname{GL}_{78}(R)$ is compatible with the twisting
and satisfies
\[
 C_0\equiv I_{78}\pmod{M_{78}(J)},\qquad
 C_0\varphi_1(x_\lambda(1))C_0^{-1}=x_\lambda(1)
 \quad(\lambda\in\Phi_\rho).
\]

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{2. Replace the linear normalization by a group element.}
At this point, $C_0$ is not known to belong to $G$.
Its transported Chevalley bracket is invariant under the standard
frame.
An integral calculation describes all frame-invariant alternating
tensors, and the Jacobi identity reduces the transported bracket
to two scalar coefficients.
We correct these coefficients over a faithfully flat local extension
without changing the normalized frame.
A local bracket-stabilizer result places the corrected matrix in
the adjoint group.
The triviality of the frame centralizer in the adjoint group over
arbitrary coefficient rings gives uniqueness and descent to $R$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{3. Recover the coefficients.}
The normalized map is now an automorphism of $E$ fixing the
standard frame. Its values preserve the Chevalley bracket.
Together with this bracket preservation, finite commutation
conditions recognize long-root elements and short-root elements
with skew parameters.
The $B_2$ relations and the fixed--skew decomposition of $R$ give
one additive coefficient map commuting with $\theta$.
A short $A_2$ relation proves multiplicativity; applying the same
argument to the inverse proves bijectivity.
Characteristicity and the trivial centralizer of $E$ give the full
adjoint result, while the central isogeny and perfectness give the
simply connected classification.

The remainder of Section~1 fixes the matrix conventions.
Sections~2--4 perform the linear normalization, and Section~5
corrects and descends the change of basis.
Section~6 recovers the coefficients and completes the classification.
It also gives coefficient recovery for frame-fixing homomorphisms
over arbitrary rings with involution, and relative normalization
for homomorphisms with a local target and prescribed standard
residual action.
head: manual

label: lemma:signed-transition-blocks
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:signed-transition-blocks}
Let $N_\rho$ be generated by the standard relative Weyl
representatives, and let $\pi:N_\rho\to W(F_4)$ be the natural
projection.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
For long roots $\lambda,\nu$ and
$\pi(n)\{\pm\lambda\}=\{\pm\nu\}$, the transition matrix in the
signed bases
\[
 \mathcal B_\lambda=(e_\lambda,-e_{-\lambda}),\qquad
 \mathcal B_\nu=(e_\nu,-e_{-\nu})
\]
belongs to $\{\pm I_2,\pm P\}$.

\item
For short roots $\mu=[\beta]$, $\nu=[\gamma]$ and
$\pi(n)\{\pm\mu\}=\{\pm\nu\}$, use
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal B_\mu
   &=(e_\beta,-e_{-\beta},
      e_{\tau\beta},-e_{-\tau\beta}),\\
 \mathcal B_\nu
   &=(e_\gamma,-e_{-\gamma},
      e_{\tau\gamma},-e_{-\tau\gamma}).
\end{aligned}
\]
With
\[
 P_4=P\oplus P,\qquad
 Q_4=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_2\\I_2&0\end{pmatrix},
\]
the transition matrix belongs to
\[
 \{\pm I_4,\pm P_4,\pm Q_4,\pm P_4Q_4\}.
\]

\item
An endomorphism with the same block $B\in M_2(R)$ on every
long-root pair space commutes with $N_\rho$ on their sum if
$BP=PB$.
The analogous assertion holds for a repeated short-root block
$A\in M_4(R)$ if
\[
 AP_4=P_4A,\qquad AQ_4=Q_4A.
\]
On the whole module, also require the Cartan block to commute
with each $S_i$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Signed transition blocks

title: Proof
body_md:
Work first in the integral Chevalley lattice.
A standard Weyl word is signed monomial on the root spaces.
If its absolute Weyl image is $w$ and
\[
 ne_\alpha=\varepsilon e_{w\alpha},\qquad
 ne_{-\alpha}=\varepsilon'e_{-w\alpha},
\]
then bracket preservation gives
\[
 h_{w\alpha}=nh_\alpha
   =[ne_\alpha,ne_{-\alpha}]
   =\varepsilon\varepsilon'h_{w\alpha}.
\]
Thus $\varepsilon'=\varepsilon$.
In the signed pair bases, the images
$\varepsilon e_\nu$ and $\varepsilon e_{-\nu}$ therefore give
$\varepsilon I_2$ and $-\varepsilon P$, respectively.

Every element of $N_\rho$ commutes with $Q$, so
$ne_{\tau\beta}=Qne_\beta$.
The short-root transition is consequently determined by the image
of $e_\beta$ and may additionally exchange the two absolute pairs.
This gives the four possibilities up to sign in \textup{(2)}.
The commutation conditions in \textup{(3)} make a repeated block
intertwine every listed transition.
All these identities remain valid after base change to $R$.
head: environment

label: lemma:surjective-reduction-G
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:surjective-reduction-G}
The reduction homomorphism $G\to G_k$ is surjective.
head: environment
name: Lifting the residual conjugator

title: Proof
body_md:
The Bruhat decomposition expresses every element of $G_k$ using
relative unipotent elements, standard Weyl representatives, and
a point of the fixed torus; see \cite{SteinbergLectures,Borel}.
The unipotent parameters lift as above, and the Weyl representatives
are constant root words.

For $U=R,k$, use the simple-root coordinates of the adjoint torus
\[
 \mathbf T_{\mathrm{ad}}(U)
   =\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb Z\Phi,U^\times).
\]
In the ordering $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_6$, its $\sigma$-fixed
points have coordinates
\[
 (a,b,c,d,\overline b,\overline a),
 \qquad a,b\in U^\times,\quad c,d\in U_0^\times,
\]
where $U_0$ is the fixed subring.
Lift $a,b$ to units of $R$ and lift $c,d$ by averaging.
The averaged lifts are still units, since their residues are
nonzero. These coordinates give a fixed torus lift.
head: environment

label: prop:reduction
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:reduction}
There exist $\widetilde u\in G$ and
$f\in\operatorname{Aut}(k,\overline{\ })$ such that the automorphism
\[
 \varphi_1:=i_{\widetilde u^{-1}}\circ\varphi
\]
satisfies
\[
 \pi_J\circ\varphi_1=f_*\circ\pi_J.
\]
In particular,
\[
 \varphi_1(a)\equiv a\pmod{M_{78}(J)}
 \qquad
 \bigl(a\in\langle\mathcal F(R)\rangle\bigr).
\]
This applies to every $x_\lambda(1)$, $w_\lambda(1)$, and
$h_\lambda(-1)$.
head: environment
name: Residual normalization

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that the residue involution is nontrivial.
The twisted field theorem
\cite[Theorem~36]{SteinbergLectures} gives inner, diagonal, and
field factors for $\overline\varphi$.
The compatible diagonal factors are represented by
$\mathbf T_{\mathrm{ad}}(k)^\sigma$:
their characters satisfy
\[
 \chi(\tau\alpha)=\overline{\chi(\alpha)}.
\]
They combine with the inner factor into conjugation by an element
$u\in G_k$.

The field factor commutes with the involution. Indeed, on a
short-root element it acts as
\[
 f_*\bigl(x_\alpha(t)x_{\tau\alpha}(\overline t)\bigr)
   =x_\alpha(f(t))x_{\tau\alpha}(f(\overline t)).
\]
Preservation of the twisted short-root subgroup and uniqueness
of the absolute root coordinates give
$f(\overline t)=\overline{f(t)}$. Thus
\[
 \overline\varphi=i_u\circ f_*,
 \qquad f\in\operatorname{Aut}(k,\overline{\ }).
\]

If the residue involution is trivial, then $E_k=G_k$ is split
of type $F_4$.
Its root and weight lattices coincide, so diagonal factors are
inner.
The field automorphism theorem
\cite[Theorem~30]{SteinbergLectures} for finite $k$, and
\cite{Humphreys1969} for infinite $k$, gives the same expression.
There is no additional graph factor in characteristic different
from two, and equivariance of $f$ is automatic.

Lift $u$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma:surjective-reduction-G} and remove
its conjugation. This gives the required residual identity.
Since $f$ fixes the prime subring, it fixes the reduction of
every element of the standard frame, and hence of every word
in that frame.
head: environment

label: lemma:finite-weyl-averaging
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:finite-weyl-averaging}
Let $\mathcal P\leq N_\rho$ be finite with
$|\mathcal P|\in R^\times$.
For any homomorphism
$\varphi:\mathcal P\to\operatorname{GL}_{78}(R)^\sigma$
satisfying $\varphi(p)\equiv p\pmod{M_{78}(J)}$, the matrix
\[
 D_{\mathcal P}
   :=\frac1{|\mathcal P|}
        \sum_{p\in\mathcal P}\varphi(p)p^{-1}
\]
is $Q$-symmetric, invertible, and congruent to $I_{78}$ modulo
$M_{78}(J)$, and
\[
 D_{\mathcal P}^{-1}\varphi(p)D_{\mathcal P}=p
 \qquad(p\in\mathcal P).
\]
head: environment
name: Finite averaging

title: Proof
head: environment

label: lemma:weyl-transport
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:weyl-transport}
Let $\mathcal N\leq N_\rho$ and suppose that
\[
 L_R=L'\oplus L,\qquad
 L=\bigoplus_{s\in\mathcal S}V_s,
\]
where $\mathcal S$ is finite.
Assume that all associated projections are $Q$-symmetric and
commute with $\mathcal D$, that $\mathcal N$ and
$\varphi(\mathcal N)$ preserve $L'$ and $L$, and that
$\mathcal N$ permutes the $V_s$ transitively.
Fix $V_0=V_{s_0}$, with stabilizer $\mathcal N_0$.
If
\[
 \varphi(a)|_{V_0}=a|_{V_0}\qquad(a\in\mathcal N_0),
\]
then there is a $Q$-symmetric
$C\equiv I_{78}\pmod{M_{78}(J)}$, equal to the identity on $L'$
and commuting with $\mathcal D$, such that
\[
 C^{-1}\varphi(n)C|_L=n|_L\qquad(n\in\mathcal N).
\]
Moreover, $C$ commutes with every $n\in\mathcal N$ for which
$\varphi(n)=n$.
head: environment
name: Transport normalization

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose $n_s\in\mathcal N$ with $n_sV_0=V_s$ and $n_{s_0}=1$.
If $p'$ and $p_s$ are the projections onto $L'$ and $V_s$, set
\[
 C=p'+\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}\varphi(n_s)n_s^{-1}p_s.
\]
The preceding observations show that $C$ is $Q$-symmetric,
commutes with $\mathcal D$, and satisfies
\[
 C|_{L'}=I,\qquad C(L)\subseteq L,\qquad
 C\equiv p'+\sum_s p_s=I_{78}\pmod{M_{78}(J)}.
\]
In particular, $C$ is invertible.

If $nV_s=V_t$, then $a=n_t^{-1}nn_s\in\mathcal N_0$.
For $v\in V_s$, the vector $n_s^{-1}v$ lies in $V_0$, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \varphi(n)Cv
   &=\varphi(n_t)\varphi(a)n_s^{-1}v\\
   &=\varphi(n_t)a n_s^{-1}v\\
   &=\varphi(n_t)n_t^{-1}nv=Cnv.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves the intertwining on $L$.
When $\varphi(n)=n$, it also proves $nC=Cn$ there.
The same holds on $L'$, since $n$ preserves $L'$ and
$C|_{L'}=I$.
head: environment

label: prop:weyl-normalization
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:weyl-normalization}
After a $Q$-symmetric basis change congruent to $I_{78}$ modulo
$M_{78}(J)$, all relative Weyl representatives and diagonal
involutions are fixed:
\[
 \varphi(w_\lambda(1))=w_\lambda(1),\qquad
 \varphi(h_\lambda(-1))=h_\lambda(-1)
 \qquad(\lambda\in\Phi_\rho).
\]
head: environment
name: Weyl normalization

label: lemma:centralizer-subgroup
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:centralizer-subgroup}
Every $C(\mathbf t)$ commutes with $N_\rho$ and with $Q$.
For $\mathbf t\in J^7$, it is invertible and congruent to $I_{78}$
modulo $M_{78}(J)$. For $\mathbf t\in(J\cap R_0)^7$, it is also
$Q$-symmetric.
head: environment
name: Allowed changes of basis

title: Proof
body_md:
The repeated root-pair blocks commute with $N_\rho$ by
Lemma~\ref{lemma:signed-transition-blocks}; the Cartan block is
scalar on each Weyl-invariant summand $H^\pm$, and commutation
for $\Pi$ was proved above.
All these endomorphisms commute with $Q$.
The remaining assertions follow from the congruence to the identity
and, for $Q$-symmetry, from $\overline{\mathbf t}=\mathbf t$.
head: environment

label: lemma:short-sector-rigidity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:short-sector-rigidity}
\label{lemma:full-short-root-normalization}
Let $X\in\operatorname{GL}_{78}(R)$ have the block form
\eqref{eq:short-initial-blocks}, satisfy $F(X)=0$, and be congruent
to $X^0$ modulo $M_{78}(J)$.
There is a unique $\mathbf t\in J^7$ such that
\[
 C(\mathbf t)X=X^0C(\mathbf t).
\]
If $X$ is $Q$-symmetric, then $\mathbf t\in(J\cap R_0)^7$.
head: environment
name: Normalization of the complete short-root matrix

title: Proof
body_md:
\smallskip
\noindent\emph{1. Determine the change of basis.}
For signed basis vectors $p,q$, write $[Z]_{p,q}$ for the
coefficient of $p$ in $Zq$.
Define $\mathbf y:M_{78}(R)\to R^7$ by taking, first, the four
entries in the $h_2$-row and the columns
\[
 e_{\alpha_2},\quad -e_{-\alpha_2},\quad
 e_{\alpha_5},\quad -e_{-\alpha_5},
\]
and then, with $p=-e_{\alpha_3+\alpha_5}$,
\[
 y_5(Z)=[Z]_{p,e_{\alpha_3}},\qquad
 y_6(Z)=[Z]_{p,-e_{-\alpha_3}},\qquad
 y_7(Z)=[Z]_{p,g^{-1}e_{\alpha_3}}.
\]
Here $g$ is the fixed Weyl word used in
Subsubsection~\ref{subsubsec:half-sum-weyl}.
The vector $g^{-1}e_{\alpha_3}$ is a signed root vector in $L_{12}$;
all seven entries are distinct allowed coordinates, up to sign.

Using $C(\mathbf t)=I_{78}+\sum_jt_jT_j$, define the
$7\times7$ matrix $M(X)$ by
\[
 M(X)_{\cdot j}=\mathbf y(T_jX-X^0T_j).
\]
The seven equations
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:seven-linear-intertwining}
 \mathbf y\bigl(C(\mathbf t)X-X^0C(\mathbf t)\bigr)=0
\end{equation}
are the linear system
\[
 M(X)\mathbf t=-\mathbf y(X-X^0).
\]
At the standard matrix, direct multiplication gives
\[
 M(X^0)\mathbf t=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 (t_5+t_6)/2\\
 (t_4-t_1)/2\\
 (t_5-t_6)/2\\
 (t_4+t_1)/2\\
 t_4-t_2-t_7/8\\
 -t_3-t_7/8\\
 -t_7/8
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \det M(X^0)=\frac1{32}.
\]
Since $M(X)\equiv M(X^0)\pmod{M_7(J)}$, the matrix $M(X)$
is invertible and the system has a unique solution
$\mathbf t\in J^7$.
The resulting $C=C(\mathbf t)$ is invertible and commutes with
the diagonal involutions and all constant matrices occurring in $F$.
Consequently,
\[
 X^*:=C^{-1}X^0C
\]
has the required block form, satisfies $F(X^*)=0$, and is congruent
to $X^0$ modulo $M_{78}(J)$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{2. Prove the full intertwining identity.}
The Jacobian $DF(X^0)$ has $788$ columns and $11402$ nonzero rows.
The exact calculation selects $781$ polynomial components
$F_{\rm sel}$ such that, after deleting the seven columns
underlying $\mathbf y$, their Jacobian gives a square matrix
$J_{\rm sq}$ with
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:short-normalization-minor}
 |\det J_{\rm sq}|=2^{200}.
\end{equation}
This certificate is contained in
\texttt{sections/section4\_complete\_short\_root/}
of \texttt{twisted\_e6\_verification.zip}.
The script \texttt{compute\_certificate.py} constructs the system
and the certificate. The coordinate and equation indexing is
recorded in \texttt{data/coordinates.json}, the row and column
selection in \texttt{data/selection.json}, and the exact minor
in \texttt{data/selected\_minor.npz}.

Let $J_{\rm sel}$ be the $781\times788$ Jacobian before deleting
columns, and let $Y_0$ represent $\mathbf y$ on the allowed
coordinates.
Each row of $Y_0$ selects one of the seven distinct coordinates
with coefficient $\pm1$.
Expanding along these rows and using
\eqref{eq:short-normalization-minor} gives
\[
 \mathcal M_0:=
 \begin{pmatrix}J_{\rm sel}\\Y_0\end{pmatrix}
 \in\operatorname{GL}_{788}(\mathbb Z[1/2]).
\]

Both $X$ and $X^*$ satisfy the selected polynomial equations.
Moreover, $CX^*=X^0C$, so
\eqref{eq:seven-linear-intertwining} gives
$\mathbf y(C(X-X^*))=0$.
Let $z\in J^{788}$ be the column of entries of $X-X^*$.
Since $X,X^*\equiv X^0$ and $C\equiv I_{78}$ modulo $J$,
polynomial finite differences give
\[
 0=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 F_{\rm sel}(X)-F_{\rm sel}(X^*)\\
 \mathbf y(C(X-X^*))
 \end{pmatrix}
 =(\mathcal M_0+\mathcal E)z,
 \qquad \mathcal E\in M_{788}(J).
\]
Indeed, factoring each polynomial difference gives coefficients
reducing to the corresponding derivatives at $X^0$; the lower
block reduces to $Y_0$.
The coefficient matrix is invertible over $R$, so $z=0$.
Hence $X=X^*$ and $CX=X^0C$.
This is a finite argument; it uses neither nilpotence of $J$
nor completeness or Henselianity.

Any intertwiner in the family satisfies the seven linear equations,
so their uniqueness proves uniqueness of $\mathbf t$.
Finally, when $X$ is $Q$-symmetric, applying $\sigma$ to the full
intertwining identity gives the same identity for
\[
 \sigma(C(\mathbf t))=C(\overline{\mathbf t}).
\]
Uniqueness implies $\overline{\mathbf t}=\mathbf t$.
head: environment

label: lemma:root-square-uniqueness
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:root-square-uniqueness}
Let $U,Y\in\operatorname{GL}_n(R)$ satisfy
\[
 (U-I_n)^3=0,\qquad
 Y\equiv U\pmod{M_n(J)},\qquad Y^2=U^2.
\]
Then $Y=U$.
head: environment
name: Uniqueness from the square

title: Proof
body_md:
Writing $U=I_n+N$, with $N^3=0$, gives
\[
 U=I_n+\frac12(Y^2-I_n)-\frac18(Y^2-I_n)^2.
\]
Thus $U$ commutes with $Y$, and $(Y-U)(Y+U)=0$.
Since $Y+U$ is congruent to the invertible matrix $2U$ modulo
$M_n(J)$, it is invertible. Hence $Y=U$.
head: environment

label: prop:root-unipotent-normalization
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:root-unipotent-normalization}
There is a matrix $C\in\operatorname{GL}_{78}(R)^\sigma$,
congruent to $I_{78}$ modulo $M_{78}(J)$ and commuting with
$N_\rho$, such that
\[
 C\varphi(x_\lambda(1))C^{-1}=x_\lambda(1)
 \qquad(\lambda\in\Phi_\rho).
\]
head: environment
name: Constant-root normalization

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply Lemma~\ref{lemma:full-short-root-normalization} to $X_{e_4}$.
It gives a $Q$-symmetric $C=C(\mathbf t)$ commuting with $N_\rho$.
Replace $\varphi$ by $i_C\circ\varphi$, retaining the notation
$X_\lambda$ for its current images.
Then $X_{e_4}=x_{e_4}(1)$ on the whole module, and $N_\rho$
remains fixed.
Transitivity of the Weyl group on short roots gives
\[
 X_\gamma=x_\gamma(1)\qquad(\gamma\in\Phi_{\rho,s});
\]
if transport gives parameter $-1$, use inversion.

Every long root is $\lambda=\gamma+\delta$ for two orthogonal
short roots, and
\[
 [x_\gamma(1),x_\delta(1)]
   =x_\lambda(2\varepsilon),
 \qquad \varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}.
\]
Applying $\varphi$ and inverting when necessary yields
\[
 X_\lambda^2=x_\lambda(1)^2.
\]
The long-root matrix $x_\lambda(1)$ is an absolute root matrix,
so $(x_\lambda(1)-I_{78})^3=0$.
Its standard residue and Lemma~\ref{lemma:root-square-uniqueness}
therefore give $X_\lambda=x_\lambda(1)$.
head: environment

label: lemma:invariant-alternating-tensors
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:invariant-alternating-tensors}
For every commutative $A$-algebra $S$, the alternating $S$-bilinear
maps $\Lambda^2L_S\to L_S$ invariant under $\mathcal F_S$ form
\[
 SB_{++}\oplus SB_{+-}\oplus SB_{--}.
\]
This description is preserved by arbitrary base change.
head: environment
name: Invariant tensors

title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to impose invariance under
$x_{\pm[\alpha_i]}(1)$, $1\leq i\leq4$:
their words give the simple Weyl representatives and diagonal
involutions, and Weyl conjugation gives the other frame elements.

Work over $A$ in a $Q$-eigenbasis adapted to the four diagonal
involutions. For an alternating tensor with coefficients $b_{ij}^k$,
invariance under a matrix $g$ means
\[
 \sum_l g_{kl}b_{ij}^l
 -\sum_{p<q}(g_{pi}g_{qj}-g_{qi}g_{pj})b_{pq}^k=0
 \qquad(i<j).
\]
Diagonal invariance removes coefficients with incompatible
characters. Since the frame commutes with $Q$, the remaining
system splits into six channels. Exact computation gives the
following ranks and kernels, with invertible square subsystems
over $A$ certifying the ranks:
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r|c}
 \text{channel}&\text{unknowns}&\text{rank}&\text{kernel}\\ \hline
 \Lambda^2L_A^+\longrightarrow L_A^+&5016&5015&AB_{++}\\
 \Lambda^2L_A^+\longrightarrow L_A^-&1932&1932&0\\
 L_A^+\otimes L_A^-\longrightarrow L_A^+&3968&3968&0\\
 L_A^+\otimes L_A^-\longrightarrow L_A^-&2320&2319&AB_{+-}\\
 \Lambda^2L_A^-\longrightarrow L_A^+&1108&1107&AB_{--}\\
 \Lambda^2L_A^-\longrightarrow L_A^-&506&506&0.
\end{array}
\]
The systems, standard tensors, and selected minors are in
\texttt{sections/section5\_invariant\_tensors/}
of \texttt{twisted\_e6\_verification.zip}.
The script \texttt{compute\_certificate.py} constructs them, and
\texttt{verify\_certificate.py} checks the stored certificates.
The variable orderings, selected rows, and retained columns are
recorded in \texttt{data/}.

In each nonzero channel, the standard tensor solves the full
system and has a unit coefficient in the sole free coordinate.
For any solution over $S$, subtract its unique multiple matching
that coordinate. The selected invertible system forces all
remaining coefficients to vanish.
In each zero channel, an invertible square subsystem forces the
entire tensor to vanish. All the inverses are defined over $A$,
so no flatness assumption on $S$ is needed.
head: environment

label: lemma:graph-matrix-not-inner
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: The frame centralizer

label: eq:bracket-generation
title: Proof
body_md:
We first establish the generation identities
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:bracket-generation}
 \langle\{L_A^+,L_A^+\}\rangle_A=L_A^+,\qquad
 \langle\{L_A^+,L_A^-\}\rangle_A=L_A^-.
\end{equation}
The root-vector parts are generated by
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \{h_\alpha,e_\alpha\}&=2e_\alpha
       &&(\tau\alpha=\alpha),\\
 \{h_\alpha+h_{\tau\alpha},
       e_\alpha\pm e_{\tau\alpha}\}
   &=2(e_\alpha\pm e_{\tau\alpha})
       &&(\tau\alpha\ne\alpha),
\end{aligned}
\]
using orthogonality in the second line.
The Cartan parts are generated by
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \{e_{\alpha_i},e_{-\alpha_i}\}&=h_i
       &&(i=3,4),\\
 \{e_{\alpha_i}+e_{\tau\alpha_i},
       e_{-\alpha_i}\pm e_{-\tau\alpha_i}\}
   &=h_i\pm h_{\tau\alpha_i}
       &&(i=1,2).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since only $2$ is inverted, these identities hold after every
base change.

If $D\in\operatorname{End}_S(L_S)$ centralizes the frame, then
$(u,v)\mapsto D\{u,v\}$ is frame-invariant.
By Lemma~\ref{lemma:invariant-alternating-tensors}, it equals
$aB_{++}+bB_{+-}+cB_{--}$.
Its restrictions to $L_S^+\times L_S^+$ and
$L_S^+\times L_S^-$, together with
\eqref{eq:bracket-generation}, give
\[
 D|_{L_S^+}=aI,\qquad D|_{L_S^-}=bI.
\]
Thus $D=a\pi_++b\pi_-$.
Conversely, these endomorphisms centralize the frame because
the frame commutes with $Q$.

Next, $Q$ does not belong to $\mathcal G(F)$ for any field $F$
with $2\in F^\times$.
Indeed, after extension to an algebraic closure, its action on
the standard maximal torus would be induced by an element of
$W(E_6)$. But this action is the nontrivial diagram automorphism:
it preserves the fundamental chamber, whose Weyl-group stabilizer
is trivial. Passing to a residue field therefore also excludes
$Q$ from $\mathcal G(S)$ for every nonzero $S$.

Finally, let $D=a\pi_++b\pi_-\in\mathcal G(S)$.
Invertibility makes $a,b$ units.
Bracket preservation and~\eqref{eq:bracket-generation} give
$a^2=a$, hence $a=1$.
The identity
\[
 \{e_{\alpha_1}-e_{\alpha_6},
       e_{-\alpha_1}-e_{-\alpha_6}\}=h_1+h_6
\]
then gives $b^2=1$.
Thus $e_-=(1-b)/2$ is an idempotent, and on the factor $e_-S$
the matrix $D$ equals $Q$.
The exclusion just proved forces $e_-S=0$, so $b=1$ and $D=I_{78}$.
head: environment

label: lemma:bracket-stabilizer-tangent
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:bracket-stabilizer-tangent}
For every commutative $A$-algebra $S$,
\[
 \operatorname{Der}_S(L_S)
   =\bigoplus_{\beta\in\Phi}S\,\operatorname{ad}e_\beta
      \ \oplus\ \bigoplus_{i=1}^6S\,\partial_i,
\]
where, for $\beta=\sum_i m_i(\beta)\alpha_i$,
\[
 \partial_i(h_j)=0,\qquad
 \partial_i(e_\beta)=m_i(\beta)e_\beta.
\]
This is the image of $\operatorname{Lie}(\mathcal G)_S$ in
$\operatorname{End}_S(L_S)$. Hence the tangent module of
$\mathcal H$ at the identity is free of rank $78$ after every
base change.
head: environment
name: Derivations of the Chevalley module

title: Proof
body_md:
For every nonzero
\[
 \delta\in(\Phi\cup\{0\})-(\Phi\cup\{0\}),
\]
we first show that some $h\in H_A$ satisfies $\delta(h)=1$.
Normalize roots to have square length $2$.
For a root $\delta$, its coroot has value $2$.
Otherwise write $\delta=\alpha-\beta$ with distinct roots.
Then
\[
 \delta(h_\alpha)=2-(\alpha,\beta)\in\{1,2,3,4\}.
\]
Only the value $3$ requires an argument.
In that case $(\delta,\delta)=6$.
If every $\delta(h_i)$ were divisible by $3$, then $\delta/3$
would be a weight of square length $2/3$.
This is impossible: the inverse Cartan matrix has positive
entries and diagonal
\[
 \left(\frac43,\frac{10}3,6,2,\frac{10}3,\frac43\right),
\]
so every nonzero dominant weight, and hence every nonzero weight,
has square length at least $4/3$.
Thus the values $\delta(h_i)$ generate the unit ideal in $A$,
proving the claim.

Use the root-lattice grading
$(L_S)_0=H_S$, $(L_S)_\beta=Se_\beta$.
Every derivation is a sum of homogeneous derivations, with degrees
among the differences considered above.
For a derivation $D_\delta$ of nonzero degree, applying it to
$\{h,v\}=\beta(h)v$ gives
\[
 \operatorname{ad}(D_\delta h)=-\delta(h)D_\delta.
\]
Choose $h$ with $\delta(h)=1$.
If $\delta\notin\Phi$, then $D_\delta h=0$ and $D_\delta=0$.
Otherwise, $D_\delta h\in Se_\delta$, so $D_\delta$ is a multiple
of $\operatorname{ad}e_\delta$.

For degree zero, write $D_0e_\beta=c_\beta e_\beta$.
The derivation identity on $\{h,e_\beta\}$ gives
$\beta(D_0h)=0$ for every root.
Also,
\[
 D_0h_i=(c_{\alpha_i}+c_{-\alpha_i})h_i.
\]
Applying $\alpha_i$ and using the unit $2$ shows that $D_0h_i=0$.
Thus $D_0H_S=0$, and the identities on opposite root vectors
give $c_{-\beta}=-c_\beta$.
Since the nonzero root-string constants are $\pm1$,
\[
 c_{\alpha+\beta}=c_\alpha+c_\beta
 \qquad(\alpha,\beta,\alpha+\beta\in\Phi).
\]
Induction on positive-root height now gives
$c_\beta=\sum_i m_i(\beta)c_{\alpha_i}$, so
$D_0=\sum_i c_{\alpha_i}\partial_i$.

The displayed derivations are independent: the root derivations
have distinct nonzero degrees and send $h_\beta$ to $-2e_\beta$,
while the $\partial_i$ are distinguished on the simple root vectors.
They are the tangent vectors of the absolute root subgroups and
of the adjoint torus
$\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb Z\Phi,\mathbb G_m)$.
Finally, substituting $I_{78}+\varepsilon D$, with $\varepsilon^2=0$,
in the equations of $\mathcal H$ identifies its tangent module
with $\operatorname{Der}_S(L_S)$.
head: environment

label: prop:local-bracket-stabilizer
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:local-bracket-stabilizer}
Let $T$ be a local commutative $A$-algebra with maximal ideal
$\mathfrak n$. If
\[
 D\in\mathcal H(T),\qquad
 D\equiv I_{78}\pmod{M_{78}(\mathfrak n)},
\]
then $D\in\mathcal G(T)$.
head: environment
name: Local bracket stabilizer

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $\mathfrak p=\ker(A\to T/\mathfrak n)$, and let $e$ be the
point of the identity section over $\mathfrak p$.
By Lemma~\ref{lemma:bracket-stabilizer-tangent}, the Jacobian
of the bracket equations at $e$ has rank
\[
 78^2-78=6006.
\]
Choose $6006$ equations with a $6006\times6006$ Jacobian minor
$\Delta$ nonzero at $e$.
On the open locus
$\mathcal V\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_{78,A}$ where $\Delta$
is invertible, their zero scheme $\mathcal Y$ is smooth over $A$
of relative dimension $78$; see
\cite[Tags 00T7 and 00T8]{StacksProject}.
There are closed immersions
\[
 \mathcal G\cap\mathcal V
   \ \subseteq\ \mathcal H\cap\mathcal V
   \ \subseteq\ \mathcal Y.
\]

Both $\mathcal G$ and $\mathcal Y$ are smooth of relative
dimension $78$ over the regular Noetherian ring $A$.
Since $e$ is a rational point of the fibre over $\mathfrak p$,
their local rings at $e$ are regular of dimension
$78+\dim A_{\mathfrak p}$.
The induced surjection
\[
 \mathcal O_{\mathcal Y,e}\longrightarrow
 \mathcal O_{\mathcal G,e}
\]
has prime kernel, because the target is a domain.
Equality of dimensions makes this prime have height zero;
the source is a domain, so the kernel is zero.

The ideal defining $\mathcal G\cap\mathcal V$ in the Noetherian
scheme $\mathcal Y$ is finitely generated. Its stalk at $e$ is zero,
so it vanishes on an open neighborhood $\mathcal U$ of $e$.
On this neighborhood all three schemes coincide.
In particular, $\mathcal U$ is an open neighborhood of $e$
in $\mathcal H$ contained in $\mathcal G$.

The morphism $\operatorname{Spec}T\to\mathcal H$ defined by $D$
sends the closed point to $e$.
The inverse image of $\mathcal U$ is an open subset containing
that closed point, hence is all of $\operatorname{Spec}T$.
Thus $D\in\mathcal G(T)$.
The Noetherian argument takes place over $A$, not over $T$.
head: environment

label: prop:descent-of-correction
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:descent-of-correction}
Suppose
\[
 C_0\in\operatorname{GL}_{78}(R)^\sigma,\qquad
 C_0\equiv I_{78}\pmod{M_{78}(J)},
\]
and every matrix
\[
 a_\lambda=C_0^{-1}x_\lambda(1)C_0
 \qquad(\lambda\in\Phi_\rho)
\]
preserves the Chevalley bracket.
There is a unique $C\in\mathcal G(R)$ satisfying
\[
 Ca_\lambda C^{-1}=x_\lambda(1)
 \qquad(\lambda\in\Phi_\rho).
\]
Moreover,
\[
 C=(r\pi_++z\pi_-)C_0
   \in G_{\mathrm{ad},\sigma}(E_6,R),\qquad
 C\equiv I_{78}\pmod{M_{78}(J)}
\]
for units $r,z\in(1+J)\cap R_0$.
head: environment

label: eq:transported-bracket-properties
title: Proof
body_md:
\smallskip
\noindent\emph{1. Determine the transported bracket.}
Put
\[
 B(u,v)=\{u,v\}_{C_0}
       :=C_0\{C_0^{-1}u,C_0^{-1}v\},\qquad
 \sigma_L(u)=Q\overline u.
\]
This is an alternating $R$-bilinear Lie bracket.
The assumptions on $C_0$ and $a_\lambda$ give
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:transported-bracket-properties}
\begin{aligned}
 B(u,v)&\equiv\{u,v\}\pmod{JL_R},\\
 B(x_\lambda(1)u,x_\lambda(1)v)
   &=x_\lambda(1)B(u,v)
       &&(\lambda\in\Phi_\rho),\\
 B(\sigma_Lu,\sigma_Lv)&=\sigma_LB(u,v).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The last identity uses $C_0\sigma_L=\sigma_LC_0$, not ordinary
commutation with $Q$.

Lemma~\ref{lemma:invariant-alternating-tensors}, together with
reduction and semilinear compatibility, yields
\[
 B=rB_{++}+sB_{+-}+tB_{--},
 \qquad r,s,t\in(1+J)\cap R_0.
\]
Jacobi on $u_+,v_+\in L_R^+$ and $w_-\in L_R^-$ gives
\[
 s(s-r)\,\bigl\{\{u_+,v_+\},w_-\bigr\}=0.
\]
For
\[
 u_+=h_1+h_6,\qquad
 v_+=e_{\alpha_1}+e_{\alpha_6},\qquad
 w_-=e_{-\alpha_1}-e_{-\alpha_6},
\]
the last bracket is $2(h_1-h_6)$.
Since $2s$ is a unit, $s=r$. Thus
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:two-bracket-coefficients}
 \{\ ,\ \}_{C_0}=rB_{++}+rB_{+-}+tB_{--},
 \qquad r,t\in(1+J)\cap R_0.
\end{equation}

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{2. Correct the bracket over a local extension.}
Set
\[
 R'=R[Z]/(Z^2-rt),\qquad
 \mathfrak m=(J,Z-1)R',\qquad
 S=R'_{\mathfrak m},\qquad \mathfrak n=\mathfrak mS,
\]
and let $z$ be the image of $Z$.
Since $rt\equiv1\pmod J$, the ideal $\mathfrak m$ is maximal and
$S/\mathfrak n\simeq R/J$.
The algebra $R'$ is free of rank two over $R$, so $R\to S$ is
flat and local, hence faithfully flat.
The involution extends by $\overline Z=Z$ and preserves
$\mathfrak m$. Consequently,
\[
 z\in S_0^\times,\qquad z\equiv1\pmod{\mathfrak n},\qquad z^2=rt.
\]

Put
\[
 K=r\pi_++z\pi_-,\qquad C=KC_0.
\]
The matrix $K$ is $Q$-symmetric, congruent to the identity, and
centralizes the frame because it is a polynomial in $Q$.
Transporting~\eqref{eq:two-bracket-coefficients} once more gives
\[
 \{\ ,\ \}_{C}
   =B_{++}+B_{+-}+\frac{rt}{z^2}B_{--}
   =\{\ ,\ \}.
\]
Thus $C\in\mathcal H(S)$ and
$C\equiv I_{78}\pmod{M_{78}(\mathfrak n)}$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:local-bracket-stabilizer} gives
$C\in\mathcal G(S)$; its $Q$-symmetry gives
$C\in G_{\mathrm{ad},\sigma}(E_6,S)$.
Since $K$ centralizes the frame,
\[
 Ca_\lambda C^{-1}=x_\lambda(1)
 \qquad(\lambda\in\Phi_\rho).
\]

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{3. Descend the correction.}
Let $C_1,C_2$ be the two pullbacks of $C$ to $S_2=S\otimes_R S$.
Both have the same conjugacies with the matrices $a_\lambda$,
which are defined over $R$.
Hence $C_2C_1^{-1}\in\mathcal G(S_2)$ centralizes $\mathcal F_{S_2}$.
Lemma~\ref{lemma:frame-centralizer} gives $C_1=C_2$, without
requiring $S_2$ to be local.
The fpqc sheaf property
\cite[Tag 023Q]{StacksProject} therefore descends $C$ uniquely
to $\mathcal G(R)$.

It follows that $K=CC_0^{-1}$ is defined over $R$.
Over $S$,
\[
 K(h_1-h_6)=z(h_1-h_6),
\]
so its $h_1$-coefficient shows that $z$ also comes from $R$.
Faithful flatness descends the identities
$\overline z=z$ and $z^2=rt$.
The latter makes $z$ a unit, and
$\mathfrak n\cap R=J$ gives $z-1\in J$.
Thus $K$ and $C$ are $Q$-symmetric and congruent to the identity
over $R$, proving the stated form of $C$.

Finally, if $C'\in\mathcal G(R)$ has the same frame conjugacies,
then $C'C^{-1}$ centralizes the frame.
Lemma~\ref{lemma:frame-centralizer} gives $C'=C$.
head: environment

label: lemma:long-root-rigidity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:long-root-rigidity}
\label{lemma:skew-root-rigidity}
For every commutative $A$-algebra $T$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Cent}_{\mathcal G(T)}(\mathcal S_{N_\alpha})
   &=\{U_\alpha(c)\mid c\in T\},\\
 \operatorname{Cent}_{\mathcal G(T)}(\mathcal S_{N_-})
   &=\{U_-(c)\mid c\in T\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The parameter is unique in both cases. If $T$ has an involution
and a recognized element $Y$ belongs to $G(T)$, its parameter lies
in $T_0$ in the first case and in $T^-$ in the second.
head: environment
name: Root recognition

label: eq:long-recognition-linear
title: Proof
body_md:
\smallskip
\noindent\emph{1. Solve the linear commutation equations.}
The diagonal decompositions of
Subsection~\ref{subsec:initial-root-decompositions} leave $836$
coordinates in the long-root case and $788$ in the short-root case.
Each family contains $33$ constant root matrices. Exact elimination
over $A$ gives, respectively,
\begin{align}
 Y&=aI_{78}+bQ+cN_\alpha+dQN_\alpha+eN_\alpha^2+uT_\alpha,
       \qquad 3u=0,
       \label{eq:long-recognition-linear}\\
 Y&=aI_{78}+bQ+cN_-+dQN_-+pN_-^2+\ell QN_-^2+uT_-.
       \label{eq:skew-recognition-linear}
\end{align}
Here $T_\alpha$ is zero except for
\[
 T_\alpha(e_{-\alpha})=-h_1+h_2-h_5+h_6,
\]
and the integral matrix $T_-$ is normalized by
\[
\begin{aligned}
 T_-(h_1)&=3(e_\beta-e_{\tau\beta}),\\
 T_-(e_{-\beta})&=2h_1+h_2-h_5-2h_6,\\
 T_-(e_{-\tau\beta})&=-2h_1-h_2+h_5+2h_6.
\end{aligned}
\]
The certificates select square subsystems of sizes $830$ and $781$
with determinants in $A^\times$.
The displayed model matrices solve these selected equations, and
the matrices taking their coefficients to the six or seven free
coordinates have determinants $-4$ and $-8$, respectively.
Thus the selected equations force the displayed forms, with unique
coefficients, after arbitrary base change.
In the long-root case, substitution in the remaining equations
gives exactly $\pm3u=0$; in the short-root case all remaining
equations vanish. In particular, the term $uT_\alpha$ cannot yet
be removed.

The systems, coordinate maps, and selected minors are in
\texttt{sections/section6\_parameter\_rigidity/}
of \texttt{twisted\_e6\_verification.zip}.
The full matrix $T_-$ is stored in \texttt{data/short\_T\_minus.npz}.
The script \texttt{compute\_certificate.py} reconstructs both
systems and checks the bracket identities used below.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{2. Impose bracket preservation.}
For either linear form,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:recognition-determinant}
 \det Y=(a+b)^{52}(a-b)^{26}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, use the integer grading defined by $h_\alpha$, or by
$h_\beta+h_{\tau\beta}$, before base change. The matrix $Q$
preserves degrees, while the terms involving $N,T_\alpha,T_-$
raise degree by two and those involving $N^2$ by four.
Thus the diagonal part is $aI_{78}+bQ$.
Invertibility of $Y$ makes $a+b$ and $a-b$ units.

Write $\Delta_Y(v,w)=Y\{v,w\}-\{Yv,Yw\}$.
In~\eqref{eq:long-recognition-linear}, the $e_{\alpha_1}$- and
$e_{\alpha_6}$-coefficients of $\Delta_Y(h_1,e_{\alpha_1})$ are
$2a(1-a)$ and $2b(1-b)$.
In~\eqref{eq:skew-recognition-linear}, the $h_1$-, $e_{-\beta}$-,
and $e_{-\tau\beta}$-coefficients of
$\Delta_Y(h_1,e_{-\beta})$ are $2u$, $a(1-a)$, and $b(1-b)$.
Hence $a^2=a$, $b^2=b$ in both cases, and $u=0$ in the short-root
case. Now
\[
 (a-b)(a+b-1)=0
\]
gives $a+b=1$, so $a,b$ are complementary idempotents and
$T=aT\times bT$.

First work on $aT$, where $a=1$, $b=0$.
In the long-root case, the $e_{\alpha_2+\alpha_3+\alpha_4}$-coefficient
of $\Delta_Y(h_1,e_{\alpha_3+\alpha_5})$ is $-d$, and the
$h_1$-coefficient of $\Delta_Y(h_3,e_{-\alpha_4})$ is $-u$.
Thus $d=u=0$.
The $e_{\alpha_4}$-coefficient of
$\Delta_Y(h_4,e_{-\alpha_4})$ is then $4(2e-c^2)$.
Thus $e=c^2/2$ and $Y=U_\alpha(c)$.

In the short-root case, the $e_\beta$-coefficient of
$\Delta_Y(h_1,e_{-\beta})$, followed by the $h_5$- and
$e_\beta$-coefficients of $\Delta_Y(h_1,e_{-\tau\beta})$, gives
\[
 2(c^2-2p)=0,\qquad -d=0,\qquad -2(cd+\ell)=0.
\]
Hence $p=c^2/2$, $d=\ell=0$, and $Y=U_-(c)$.
Only powers of two have been cancelled.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{3. Exclude the graph factor and recover the parameter.}
On $bT$, apply the preceding calculations to $QY$.
The matrix $Q$ preserves the bracket and commutes with
$\mathcal S_N$, and multiplication by $Q$ interchanges the
coefficients $a,b$. Thus $QY=U_\alpha(c')$ or $U_-(c')$ on
this factor. Since both $Y$ and the resulting root element
belong to $\mathcal G(bT)$, a nonzero factor $bT$ would give
$Q\in\mathcal G(bT)$, contrary to
Lemma~\ref{lemma:frame-centralizer}.
Therefore $b=0$, proving the asserted forms.
The reverse inclusions follow from the definition of $\mathcal S_N$.

The root-coordinate formulas make each parameter unique. Finally,
\[
 \sigma(U_\alpha(c))=U_\alpha(\overline c),\qquad
 \sigma(U_-(c))=U_-(-\overline c).
\]
For $Y\in G(T)$, uniqueness gives $c\in T_0$ or $c\in T^-$,
respectively.
head: environment

label: prop:fixed-frame-homomorphisms
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:fixed-frame-homomorphisms}
Let $S,T$ be commutative rings with involution and with $2$
invertible. If a homomorphism
\[
 \Psi:E(S)\longrightarrow G(T)
\]
satisfies $\Psi(x_\lambda(1))=x_\lambda(1)$ for every relative
root, then there is a unique unital equivariant ring homomorphism
$\rho:S\to T$ such that
\[
 \Psi(x_\lambda(t))=x_\lambda(\rho(t))
\]
for every admissible parameter. In particular, $\Psi=\rho_*$ and
$\Psi(E(S))\subseteq E(T)$.
If $\Psi:E(S)\to E(T)$ is an isomorphism, then $\rho$ is an
isomorphism of rings with involution.
head: environment
name: Homomorphisms fixing the frame

title: Proof
body_md:
The Weyl and diagonal words in the frame are also fixed.
Write $X_\lambda(t)=\Psi(x_\lambda(t))$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Long roots.}
For $s\in S_0$, the element $x_\alpha(s)$ commutes with
$\mathcal S_{N_\alpha}$. Applying $\Psi$ and
Lemma~\ref{lemma:long-root-rigidity} gives
\[
 X_\alpha(s)=x_\alpha(\rho_0(s)),\qquad \rho_0(s)\in T_0.
\]
Faithful parametrization and the root-subgroup law make $\rho_0$
additive, with $\rho_0(1)=1$. Fixed Weyl conjugation gives the
same map on every long root.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Short roots.}
For fixed signs $\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\in\{1,-1\}$,
\[
 [x_{e_3-e_4}(s),x_{e_4}(1)]
   =x_{e_3}(\varepsilon_1s)
      x_{e_3+e_4}(\varepsilon_2s)
 \qquad(s\in S_0).
\]
Apply $\Psi$ and compare with the same commutator over $T$.
Cancelling the recognized long-root factor gives
$X_{e_3}(s)=x_{e_3}(\rho_0(s))$ for $s\in S_0$.
For $q\in S^-$, the equality $x_{e_3}(q)=U_-(q)$ and
Lemma~\ref{lemma:skew-root-rigidity} similarly give
\[
 X_{e_3}(q)=x_{e_3}(\rho_-(q)),\qquad \rho_-(q)\in T^-,
\]
where $\rho_-$ is additive. Define
\[
 \rho(t)=\rho_0\!\left(\frac{t+\overline t}{2}\right)
        +\rho_-\!\left(\frac{t-\overline t}{2}\right).
\]
Then $\rho$ is additive and equivariant, with $\rho(1)=1$.
The root-subgroup law gives
$X_{e_3}(t)=x_{e_3}(\rho(t))$ for all $t\in S$.
Weyl transitions replace a parameter by $\pm t$ or
$\pm\overline t$, so the same formula holds on every short root.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Multiplication and uniqueness.}
In the short $A_2$ subsystem generated by $\beta_0,e_4$, the
paired absolute coordinates of Section~1 give
\[
 [x_{\beta_0}(t),x_{e_4}(u)]
   =x_{\beta_0+e_4}(\varepsilon tu)
 \qquad(t,u\in S)
\]
for a fixed sign $\varepsilon$.
Applying $\Psi$ and using faithful parametrization yields
$\rho(tu)=\rho(t)\rho(u)$.
Since the root subgroups generate $E(S)$, we have $\Psi=\rho_*$;
one short-root subgroup determines $\rho$ uniquely.
If $\Psi$ is an isomorphism onto $E(T)$, the same argument applied
to $\Psi^{-1}$ gives $\rho':T\to S$.
Evaluation of the two inverse identities on a short-root subgroup
gives $\rho'\rho=1$ and $\rho\rho'=1$.
head: environment

label: theorem:automorphisms-of-E
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{theorem:automorphisms-of-E}
\label{thm:elementary-adjoint-automorphisms}
Every automorphism of $E=E'_{\mathrm{ad},\sigma}(E_6,R)$ has a
unique expression
\[
 \varphi=i_g\circ\rho_*,\qquad
 g\in G,\quad \rho\in\operatorname{Aut}(R,\theta).
\]
Conversely, every such expression defines an automorphism of $E$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Proposition~\ref{prop:fixed-frame-homomorphisms} applied to the
normalized automorphism $\psi$ gives $\psi=\rho_*$ for
$\rho\in\operatorname{Aut}(R,\theta)$.
Since $\varphi_1=i_{\widetilde u^{-1}}\circ\varphi$ and
$\psi=i_C\circ\varphi_1$, we obtain
\[
 \varphi=i_{\widetilde uC^{-1}}\circ\rho_*.
\]
Faithful short-root parametrization also shows that the reduction
of $\rho$ is the automorphism $f$ from
Proposition~\ref{prop:reduction}.

If $i_g\circ\rho_*=i_{g'}\circ\rho'_*$, then $g'^{-1}g$
centralizes the frame, because both ring automorphisms fix it.
Lemma~\ref{lemma:frame-centralizer} gives $g=g'$, and evaluation
on a short-root subgroup gives $\rho=\rho'$.
The converse follows from normality of $E$ in $G$ and
coefficientwise functoriality.
head: environment

label: corollary:automorphisms-of-G
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By characteristicity from Section~2, restrict to $E$ and remove
the standard automorphism supplied by
Theorem~\ref{theorem:automorphisms-of-E}.
The remaining automorphism $\Xi$ fixes $E$ pointwise. For
$a\in G$ and $e\in E$, normality gives
\[
 \Xi(a)e\Xi(a)^{-1}=\Xi(aea^{-1})=aea^{-1}.
\]
Thus $a^{-1}\Xi(a)$ centralizes $E$, and hence the frame.
Lemma~\ref{lemma:frame-centralizer} gives $\Xi=1$.
Uniqueness follows by restriction to $E$.
head: environment

label: thm:simply-connected-automorphisms
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:simply-connected-automorphisms}
Every automorphism of $\widetilde E$ has the form
\[
 \varphi=i_x\circ d_\chi\circ\rho_*,
 \qquad x\in\widetilde E,\quad
 \chi\in\operatorname{Hom}_1(\Lambda_r,R^\times),\quad
 \rho\in\operatorname{Aut}(R,\theta),
\]
where $d_\chi$ is the diagonal automorphism associated with $\chi$.
Conversely, every such composition is an automorphism of
$\widetilde E$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\smallskip
\noindent\emph{1. Pass to the adjoint quotient.}
The central isogeny gives a surjection
$\delta:\widetilde E\to E$, since it preserves the parameters
of every relative root generator.
Its kernel is central, and centerlessness of $E$ gives
\[
 \ker\delta=Z(\widetilde E).
\]
Thus $\varphi$ induces an automorphism $i_g\circ\rho_*$ of $E$
by Theorem~\ref{theorem:automorphisms-of-E}.
The fixed torus normalizes $E$, so write
\[
 g=Xh(\chi),\qquad X\in E,\quad
 \chi\in\operatorname{Hom}_1(\Lambda_r,R^\times),
\]
and choose $x\in\widetilde E$ with $\delta(x)=X$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{2. Realize the diagonal factor.}
Use the group-algebra construction of
\cite[Section~9]{BuninaMakadiya2A}:
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \varepsilon_\chi:R[\Lambda_r]\longrightarrow R,\qquad
 \varepsilon_\chi(e^\alpha)=\chi(\alpha),\\
 S_\chi=R[\Lambda_{\mathrm{sc}}]
       \otimes_{R[\Lambda_r],\,\varepsilon_\chi}R.
\end{gathered}
\]
Coset representatives for $\Lambda_{\mathrm{sc}}/\Lambda_r$
containing $0$ give an $R$-basis of $S_\chi$.
Thus $S_\chi$ is free of rank three and $R\to S_\chi$ is injective.
The semilinear lattice involution descends to $S_\chi$, and
\[
 \chi'(\lambda)=e^\lambda\otimes1
 \qquad(\lambda\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{sc}})
\]
is an equivariant character extending $\chi$.
The element $h'=h(\chi')\in T_{\mathrm{sc},\sigma}(E_6,S_\chi)$
satisfies
\[
 h'x_{[\alpha]}(t)(h')^{-1}
   =x_{[\alpha]}(\chi(\alpha)t).
\]
The new parameter is admissible over $R$: for a long root,
$\chi(\alpha)\in R_0^\times$, and for a short root,
$\chi(\tau\alpha)=\overline{\chi(\alpha)}$.
The same holds for conjugation by $(h')^{-1}$.
Through the faithful base-change embedding, these conjugations
therefore define an automorphism $d_\chi$ of $\widetilde E$,
whose action depends only on $\chi$.
Neither \'etaleness of $S_\chi/R$ nor invertibility of $3$ is needed.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{3. Eliminate the central correction.}
The automorphism
$\varphi^{\mathrm{st}}=i_x\circ d_\chi\circ\rho_*$
induces the same automorphism of $E$ as $\varphi$.
Consequently,
\[
 (\varphi^{\mathrm{st}})^{-1}\varphi(y)=yz(y),
 \qquad z(y)\in Z(\widetilde E),
\]
where centrality makes $z:\widetilde E\to Z(\widetilde E)$ a
group homomorphism.

The group $\widetilde E$ is perfect: long and short $A_2$
subsystems express root elements of the corresponding length as
commutators with parameters $\pm t,1$ and constants $\pm1$.
Here $t\in R_0$ for long roots and $t\in R$ for short roots.
Weyl conjugation reaches every root, so every elementary generator
is a commutator.
Thus $z=1$ and $\varphi=\varphi^{\mathrm{st}}$.
Strictly inner and ring automorphisms, together with the construction
of $d_\chi$ above, also prove the converse.

label: prop:relative-local-normalization
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:relative-local-normalization}
Let $S$ be a commutative ring with involution and $T$ a local
commutative ring with involution, with $2$ invertible in both.
Put
\[
 \mathfrak n=\operatorname{Jac}(T),\qquad
 q:T\longrightarrow\overline T:=T/\mathfrak n,
\]
and give $\overline T$ the induced involution.
Suppose that a homomorphism $\Psi:E(S)\to E(T)$ satisfies
\[
 q_*\circ\Psi=i_h\circ(\nu_0)_*,
 \qquad h\in G(\overline T),
\]
for a unital equivariant ring homomorphism $\nu_0:S\to\overline T$.
Then there exist a unique element $g\in G(T)$ and a unique
unital equivariant ring homomorphism $\rho:S\to T$ such that
\[
 q_*(g)=h,\qquad q\circ\rho=\nu_0,\qquad
 \Psi=i_g\circ\rho_*.
\]
The element $g$ is already uniquely determined by
\[
 g\,x_{\lambda,T}(1)\,g^{-1}
   =\Psi(x_{\lambda,S}(1))
 \qquad(\lambda\in\Phi_\rho),
\]
where the second subscript specifies the coefficient ring.
Neither $\Psi$ nor $\nu_0$ is assumed injective or surjective.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lemma:surjective-reduction-G}, lift $h$ to
$\widetilde h\in G(T)$ and put
$\Psi_1=i_{\widetilde h^{-1}}\circ\Psi$.
Then $q_*\circ\Psi_1=(\nu_0)_*$, so all frame images have standard
reductions.

The common integral Weyl model from
Subsection~\ref{subsec:initial-weyl-family} and the homomorphism
versions of the normalizations in Sections~3--4 give
\[
\begin{gathered}
 C_0\in\operatorname{GL}_{78}(T)^\sigma,\qquad
 C_0\equiv I_{78}\pmod{M_{78}(\mathfrak n)},\\
 C_0\Psi_1(x_{\lambda,S}(1))C_0^{-1}=x_{\lambda,T}(1)
 \qquad(\lambda\in\Phi_\rho).
\end{gathered}
\]
The matrices $\Psi_1(x_{\lambda,S}(1))$ belong to $E(T)$ and
preserve the bracket. Proposition~\ref{prop:descent-of-correction}
therefore replaces $C_0$ by $C\in G(T)$ with the same congruence
and frame conjugacies.

Set $g=\widetilde hC^{-1}$.
Then $q_*(g)=h$, and
$\Psi^0:=i_{g^{-1}}\circ\Psi=i_C\circ\Psi_1$ fixes the frame.
Proposition~\ref{prop:fixed-frame-homomorphisms} gives
$\Psi^0=\rho_*$ for a unique unital equivariant ring homomorphism
$\rho:S\to T$.
Since $q_*\circ\Psi^0=(\nu_0)_*$, evaluation on a short-root
subgroup gives $q\circ\rho=\nu_0$.

Any other factorization has the same frame conjugacies, because
unital coefficient homomorphisms fix the frame.
Lemma~\ref{lemma:frame-centralizer} makes its conjugating element
equal to $g$; faithful short-root parametrization then makes its
coefficient homomorphism equal to $\rho$.
